the schedule-induced polydipisa phenomenon is not a unitary phenomenon, but rather is composed of two independent and separable components, one of which is the result of a behavioral sequence of which the rat is a normal participant, and the second of which is the consequence of the imposition by the experimenter of an experimental condition which is not normally encountered by the rat in its natural habitat.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
schedule-induced polydipisa is a result of the eat-then drink sequence of behavior, and schedule-induced hyperphasia is a result of a drink-then-eats sequence of behavior.

schedule-induced polydypsia and schedule-induced hyperphasia are not specific behavioral effects of time-dependent food reinforcement schedules, but are rather the behavioral consequences of the experimental manipulation of a normally occurring eat-then-drinks sequence of behavior.
schedule-induced polydipisa and hyperphagia are not specific to desalivate animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is the experimenter, not the rat, who determines the size of a meal.

the instatement and maintenance of schedule-induced behavior may be more dependent upon the experimenter's determination of meal size than on the natural behavioral sequence in which the animal normally engages.
the schedule of reinforcement is a more potent determinant of behavior than is the species-typical behavioral sequence of behavior.
